setup.caption: 1. Soak the moong overnight. Then keep them in a wet cloth.

setup.art: A child's fingers holding a sprouted moong bean with a white tail against a paper strip, with a pencil mark where the tail ends.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the longest sprout on a paper strip. Mark where the tail ends.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a line across the bottom and three paper strips of growing height standing on the line, labelled Day 3, Day 4 and Day 5.
setup.caption: 3. Paste each day's strip on the start line.

flow.do: 1. On day 1, in the evening, soak about 20 moong beans. 2. Draw a line across the bottom of the chart paper. 3. On day 2, pour off the water and wrap the beans in a wet cloth. 4. Ask for a guess: how long will a sprout be in three days?
flow.say: These beans will wake up and grow tails. Show me with your fingers how long a tail will be in three days.
flow.kid: Soak the moong beans. Next morning, wrap them in a wet cloth. Guess how long they will grow.
flow.parent: Keep the cloth damp, not dripping. In warm weather small white tails show by the morning of day 3. In cool weather they can take a day longer.

chart.title: What a finished chart can look like (yours will be your own)

flow.context: These are days 1 and 2 of the Sprout Strip Chart, a five-day project. You soak moong beans and wrap them in a wet cloth so that they sprout.

flow.do: 1. On days 3 and 4, your child picks the longest sprout. 2. Hold its tail gently along a paper strip, one end at the strip's end. 3. Mark where the tail stops, and cut there. 4. Paste the strip standing on the start line. Write the day under it.
flow.say: Find the longest sprout. Lay the tail along the strip, starting at the end. I will cut where the tail stops.
flow.kid: Find the longest sprout. Lay their tail on the strip. Paste the strip on the line.
flow.wait: Do this on day 3 and again on day 4.

ask.q: Is today's strip longer than yesterday's? How can you tell?
good: They start at the same line and today's goes further.

flow.parent: A curved tail must be straightened gently along the strip. If no tails have come by day 3, wait one more day and start the chart then.
flow.context: These are days 3 and 4 of the Sprout Strip Chart, a five-day project with sprouting moong beans. Each day you cut a paper strip as long as the longest sprout's tail.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, cut and paste the last strip. 2. Ask which strip is the shortest and which is the longest. 3. Ask what your child thinks tomorrow's strip would look like, and why.
flow.say: Look at your three strips. What happened to the length each day? What would tomorrow's strip look like?
flow.kid: Paste the last strip. Which is longest? What would tomorrow's strip look like?

ask.q: Why do all the strips stand on one line?
good: So that we can compare them.

check.q: Three strips stand on one line. How do you find the longest?
options: The one whose top is highest
check.why: The one whose top is highest. All the strips start on the same line, so the top that reaches furthest belongs to the longest strip. The strip pasted last is often the longest here, but only because the sprout grew.

flow.context: This is day 5 of the Sprout Strip Chart, a five-day project with sprouting moong beans. You paste the last strip and read the chart.

challenges.title: Stretch: will it fit? Compare two things that cannot move
challenges.context: This is a design challenge that goes past Class 1. You must find out whether a table would fit through a doorway, without moving the table. You invent a way to carry the table's length to the door.
challenges.problem: A table stands in one room. A doorway is in another part of the house. Is the table narrower than the doorway, so that it could go straight through? You may not move the table.
constraints: The table stays where it is. The door stays where it is.
No ruler and no measuring tape.
You must be sure of your answer, and able to show someone why.
materials: a ball of wool or string
a table (or a big box or a chair) and a doorway
a steel tumbler, for the last step
general: Cut a string as long as the table is wide. Carry the string to the doorway and hold it across.
Hold a broomstick across the table and pinch it where the table ends. Carry the stick to the door, still pinching.
creative: Count how many of your hand spans fit across the table. Then count hand spans across the doorway. Use the same hand each time.
Tape sheets of newspaper together until they are as wide as the table. Carry the paper to the door.
Hold your arms as wide as the table and walk to the door. Then test whether your arms stayed still on the way.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to carry the table's length to the door. Use it. Then check it with a second way. If the two ways disagree, find out why.

setup.art: A small dining table in one room and an open doorway seen across a hall, with a child looking from one to the other.
setup.caption: 1. Guess: is the table narrower than the doorway?

setup.art: A child and a grown-up holding a piece of wool across the width of a table top, with scissors ready at the table's edge.
setup.caption: 2. One way: cut a string as wide as the table.

setup.art: The child holding the same wool across the doorway, with a gap of a hand's width left over at one side.
setup.caption: 3. Carry the string to the doorway. Does it fit?

flow.do: 1. Stand where your child can see the table. Then walk to the doorway. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Ask how they could be sure without moving the table.
flow.say: Would the table go straight through this doorway? Why do you think so? How could we be sure?
flow.kid: Look at the table. Look at the door. Would the table fit through? Guess.

ask.q: Why can we not line them up at a start line?

chart.title: A table and a doorway: which is wider?

flow.context: This is the first step of the challenge Will It Fit? You guess whether a table is narrower than a doorway, without moving the table.

flow.do: 1. Ask for ideas. 2. Read the usual ways and the creative ways aloud, if your child wants ideas. 3. Let your child choose one way.
flow.say: The table cannot go to the door. What could go from the table to the door for us?
flow.kid: The table cannot move. What could you carry from the table to the door?

ask.q: How could a string help?
good: Make it as long as the table.
Take the string to the door.

flow.context: This is step 2 of the challenge Will It Fit?, where a table must be compared with a doorway. Here you think of ways to carry the table's length.

flow.do: 1. Your child uses their way. Help with cutting. 2. At the doorway, ask what the string shows. 3. Check with a second way. 4. If you can, test for real with a light table or box.
flow.say: The string is as long as the table is wide. Now hold it across the doorway. What does it tell us?
flow.kid: Use your way. Carry the length to the door. Does the table fit?

chart.title: The string matches the table

flow.parent: The string is a go-between. It is as long as the table, so whatever is true of the string at the door is true of the table.

check.q: A string is as long as the table is wide. The doorway is wider than the string. Will the table fit?
check.why: Yes. The table and the string are the same length, and the doorway is wider than the string. So the doorway is wider than the table too. Picking 'you cannot tell' means not yet trusting the string to stand in for the table.

flow.context: This is step 3 of the challenge Will It Fit?, where a table must be compared with a doorway. Here you test your own way.

flow.do: 1. Show the steel tumbler. Ask which is longer: its height, or the way round its rim. 2. Write the guess. 3. Your child wraps a string once round the rim. Cut it. 4. Stand the string up beside the tumbler.
flow.say: Which is longer: how tall this tumbler is, or the way round its top? Guess, then check with a string.
flow.kid: Which is longer: up the tumbler, or round its top? Guess. Check with a string.

ask.q: Were you surprised? Why did the height look longer?
good: The round way is bent, so it hides.

flow.parent: For an ordinary steel tumbler the way round is about twice the height, or more. Most people, grown-ups too, guess that the height is longer.
flow.context: This is the last step of the challenge Will It Fit? You use a string to compare a tumbler's height with the way round its rim.

items.p: Which ribbon is longer?
items.why: B. Both ribbons start at the same line, and B goes on further.

items.p: Which stick is the shortest?
items.why: B. All three start at the same line, and B stops first.

items.p: Straw A and straw B are the same length.
items.why: True. They start at the same line and they stop at the same place.

items.p: Write taller or shorter: A giraffe is ____ than a goat.
items.why: Taller. Both stand on the ground, and the giraffe's head is much higher up.

items.p: You want to compare two pencils. What do you do first?
opts: Line up one end of each
items.why: Line up one end of each. Then the other ends show which is longer. Held far apart, your eyes can get it wrong.

items.p: You slide a straw forward. Now the straw is longer.
items.why: False. Sliding does not add anything to the straw. It sticks out in front and falls behind at the back.

items.p: Put the ribbons in order, shortest first.
items.why: B stops first, then C, then A. So the order is B, C, A.

items.p: Which word do we use: tall or long?
items.why: We say tall for things that stand up from the ground. We say long for things that lie along the ground. Both words tell about length.

items.p: Match each thing to the word that fits best.
items.why: Deep, high, long and tall all tell how far it is from one end to the other. The word changes with the direction.

items.p: Draw a long snake and a short snake. Start both at one line.
items.a: Two snakes that start at the same line, one clearly going further than the other.
items.why: A strong drawing has both snakes starting at one line. Then anyone can see which one is longer.

items.p: Draw yourself and someone taller than you, standing on the same floor.
items.a: Two people with their feet on one line, and the other person's head higher.
items.why: The floor is the start line. The person whose head is higher is taller.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. Why did the pushed straw look longer in the Line-Up Test?
items.a: Because its front end stuck out. But its back end was behind, so it was not longer.
items.why: A strong answer talks about both ends. The straw stuck out at one end and fell short at the other.

items.p: Put the sticks in order, shortest first.
items.why: C stops first, then A, then D, then B. In order they make a staircase.

items.p: Write A or B: Bead chain ____ is longer.
items.why: B. Every bead is the same size, and both chains start at the same line. B has more beads, so it goes further.

items.p: Chain B is ____ beads longer than chain A.
items.why: 3. Chain A has 6 beads and chain B has 9. Count on from 6: 7, 8, 9. That is 3 more beads.

items.p: Meena is taller than Ravi. Ravi is taller than Anu. Who is the shortest?
items.why: Anu. Ravi is shorter than Meena, and Anu is shorter still. In order they are Anu, Ravi, Meena.

items.p: A string lies in loops. What must you do before you compare it with a pencil?
items.why: Pull it straight, with one end at the start line. A looped string hides part of its length.

items.p: A pencil standing up is longer than the same pencil lying down.
items.why: False. It is the same pencil with the same length. Only the way it points has changed.

items.p: The same pencil can be the longer one in one pair and the shorter one in another pair.
items.why: True. A pencil is longer than an eraser and shorter than a broom. Long and short are words for comparing.

items.p: Which stick is neither the longest nor the shortest?
items.why: C. A is the shortest and B is the longest. C comes in between.

items.p: Is it longer or shorter than your own arm?
items.why: A toothbrush, a matchstick and a key would stop before your fingertips. A bus, a broom and a bed go on well past them.

items.p: Draw three pencils in a staircase, from shortest to longest. Start all three at one line.
items.a: Three pencils starting at one line, each longer than the one before.
items.why: In a strong drawing the far ends climb like steps, and the starting ends are level.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. A ribbon's end sticks out further. What would you check?
items.a: I would check that both ribbons start at the same line and are pulled straight.
items.why: A strong answer looks at the other end. A ribbon can stick out only because it started ahead.

items.p: A pencil stands in a tumbler. Two children talk about it.

views.says: It is tall. It points up.
It is long. It is a pencil, and pencils are long.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other child has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says both words tell about the same length of the same pencil.
items.why: Both are right. Tall and long both tell how far it is from one end to the other. Tall also says that it points up.

items.p: A string is as long as a table. The doorway is wider than the string. Will the table fit through?
items.why: Yes. The table matches the string, and the doorway is wider than the string. So the doorway is wider than the table.

items.p: Rope A is longer than rope B. Rope B and rope C are the same length. Which is true?
opts: A and C are the same
items.why: A is longer than C. C matches B, and A is longer than B. So A is longer than C as well.

items.p: One chain has 12 beads. Another has 8 beads. The long chain has ____ more beads.
items.why: 4. Take 8 away from 12 and 4 are left. The long chain goes on for 4 more beads.

items.p: Count the squares. Strip B is ____ squares longer than strip A.
items.why: 3. Strip A is 5 squares long and strip B is 8 squares long. From 5, count on to 8: that is 3 more.

items.p: Your shadow is longer early in the morning than it is at noon.
items.why: True. In the early morning the Sun is low and shadows are long. At noon the Sun is high and shadows are short.

items.p: In the test, desert ants given longer legs stopped before they reached the nest.
items.why: False. They walked past the nest. Each step was longer, so the same steps took them too far.

items.p: Put these in order, shortest first.
items.why: A matchstick is shorter than your finger. A toothbrush is about as long as your hand. A bat is as long as your leg or more. A bus is longer than a room.

items.p: Match each word to its opposite.
items.why: Each pair tells about length in one direction: along, up or down. One word is for a lot of it and the other for a little.

items.p: Amma's muzham is longer than Kavya's. Each cuts one muzham of flowers. Who has more?
items.why: Amma. A muzham is as long as the arm that measures it. A longer arm cuts a longer string.

items.p: Draw a wiggly string that looks short. Then draw the same string pulled straight.
items.a: A wiggly line, and below it a clearly longer straight line starting at the same place.
items.why: In a strong drawing the straight string reaches further than the wiggly one did, because the bends have been pulled out.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. Which is longer: round a tumbler, or up it? How would you check?
items.a: Wrap a string once round the tumbler and cut it. Then stand the string up beside the tumbler.
items.why: A strong answer uses a string, or a strip of paper, to carry the round length and make it straight.

items.p: Two thinkers talk about a stick.

views.says: The stick has its own length, whoever looks at it.
Nothing is long by itself. It is long only next to something shorter.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other thinker has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason from the unit. For example: the straw kept its length when it was moved, or the pencil was long next to an eraser and short next to a broom.
items.why: Both have a point. The stick's length stays the same when you move it. But the words long and short are for comparing.

quiz.why: B. Both start at the same line, and B stops first. Picking A means choosing the longer one.

quiz.p: Look at the picture. Ribbon A is longer than ribbon B.
quiz.why: False. They start together and stop together, so they are the same length.

quiz.p: Write A or B: Bead chain ____ is the longer one.
quiz.why: B. The beads are all one size and both chains start at the same line. B goes further.

quiz.p: What must you do before you compare two spoons?
opts: Put one end of each at the same line
quiz.why: Put one end of each at the same line. Then the far ends show which is longer. Far apart, a look can fool you.

quiz.p: Two ribbons start at the same line. How do you tell which is longer?
quiz.why: Look at the other ends. The ribbon whose end goes further is the longer one.

quiz.p: Two straws match. You push one ahead. Now that straw is longer.
quiz.why: False. It only moved. It sticks out in front and falls short at the back. Lined up again, the straws match.

quiz.p: A string is curled up. You pull it straight. What happened to its length?
quiz.why: It stayed the same. The curl was hiding the length. Picking 'it got longer' mixes up the room a string takes with its length.

quiz.p: A pencil stands up. Then it lies down. What changed?
quiz.why: Only the way it points. Tall and long are two words for the same length.

quiz.p: Which word fits a coconut tree best?
quiz.why: Tall. We say tall for a thing that stands up a long way from the ground. Deep is for going down, as in a well.

quiz.p: Put the four sticks in order, from shortest to longest.
quiz.why: B stops first, then D, then A, then C. The far ends climb like stairs.

quiz.p: Asha is taller than Bala. Bala is taller than Chitra. Who is the tallest?
quiz.why: Asha. She is taller than Bala, and Bala is taller than Chitra. So Asha is taller than both.

quiz.p: A string is as long as a table. The string is longer than the doorway is wide. Will the table fit?
quiz.why: No. The table matches the string, and the string is wider than the doorway. So the table is wider than the doorway.

quiz.p: A string can carry the length of a table to another room.
quiz.why: True. Cut the string to match the table. Wherever the string goes, it is still as long as the table.

open_questions.q: How does a desert ant keep track of her steps?
open_questions.why_open: The 2006 test showed that the length of her steps matters. How her body and brain add the steps up is still not known.

open_questions.q: Why does a standing line look longer than a lying line of the same length?
open_questions.why_open: Adolf Fick wrote about this in 1851. Scientists have several ideas, but they still do not fully agree on the reason.

open_questions.q: What is a young child thinking when they say a pushed stick has become longer?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists say the child truly sees it as longer. Others say the child is answering a different question, such as 'which one reaches further?' The tests have not settled it.

open_questions.q: Is there a shortest length that anything can have?
open_questions.why_open: You can cut a string in half again and again. Some physicists think there may be a smallest length that cannot be cut further. Nobody has been able to test it.

maths.problem: Three ladles hang with their tops on one rod. Put them in order, shortest first.
maths.explain: All three start at the rod, so the rod is the start line. B stops first, then C, then A.
maths.context: In the Spoon Staircase you put five kitchen things in order of length. This is the same job with three ladles.
maths.why_maths: Putting lengths in order is the same thinking as putting numbers in order: each one comes after everything smaller.

chart.title: Three ladles on one rod

maths.problem: A pencil is longer than a spoon. The spoon is longer than a key. You have not lined up the pencil and the key. Which of those two is longer?
maths.explain: The key is shorter than the spoon, and the spoon is shorter than the pencil. So the key must be shorter than the pencil too. You know it without lining them up.
maths.context: In the Line-Up Test you compared things two at a time at the edge of a book. This asks what two line-ups can tell you about a third pair.
maths.why_maths: Reasoning from two things you know to a third saves you from checking every pair.

chart.title: What you lined up first

answer_chart.title: All three at one start line

maths.problem: In the tie-break of Longer Wins, Kavya's train is 9 squares long. Arun's train is 6 squares long. How many squares longer is Kavya's train?
maths.explain: Both trains start at the same line. Arun's stops at 6. Kavya's goes on to 9. Count on from 6: 7, 8, 9. That is 3 more squares.
maths.context: In the game Longer Wins, Shorter Wins, a tie is settled by laying strips end to end in a train. This asks how much longer one train is.
maths.why_maths: Taking away tells you how much longer one thing is, not only which one is longer.

maths.problem: A sprout's strips were 2, 4 and 6 squares long on three days. If the sprout keeps growing in the same way, how long will the next strip be?
maths.explain: Each strip is 2 squares longer than the one before: 2, 4, 6. Two more than 6 is 8. A real sprout may not keep to the pattern, so check with the real one.
maths.context: In the Sprout Strip Chart you pasted one paper strip a day, each as long as a moong sprout. This asks you to guess the next strip from the ones before.
maths.why_maths: Seeing how much a length grows each day lets you guess the next day before it comes.

chart.title: The sprout's strips so far

answer_chart.title: If the sprout keeps growing by 2 squares

maths.problem: You hold both ends of a string in one hand and cut the bottom of the loop. Are the two pieces the same length? Why?
maths.answer: Yes, they are the same length.
maths.explain: Both pieces start together at your fingers and end together at the cut. Two things that start together and end together are the same length. Each piece is half of the string.
maths.context: In A Muzham of Malli you cut and compared strings. This asks what happens when one string is folded and cut at the fold.
maths.why_maths: Folding lines up the two halves for you, so you can make two equal lengths without measuring.

roots.context: We lined up straws, spoons and strings. Now let us think about the words long and tall, and where they come from.

deep_truth.truth: In One Pencil, Two Words, you stood a pencil up and called it tall. You laid it down and called it long. The pencil did not change. Tall and long are two words for one thing: how far it is from end to end. People made the two words.
deep_truth.habit: We use different words, so we think tall and long are different things. The words only tell which way the thing is pointing.
deep_truth.evidence: In One Pencil, Two Words, a string cut to your height while you stood also matched you from heel to head while you lay on the floor.

three.who_am_i: Standing up, you are tall. Lying in bed, you are long. You are the same you, with the same length.
three.what_is_life: A coconut tree grows tall. A pumpkin creeper grows long. Each one is adding to their own length, in their own direction.
three.what_is_this_world: A well is deep, a tree is tall and a road is long. Each time, we mean how far it is from one end to the other.

roots.thread: Length is one idea. People gave it many names: long, tall, high, deep, wide. A lotus stalk is as long as the pond is deep. The stalk and the pond share one length, and we use two words for it.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar, the Tamil poet, says that the stalk of a water flower is as long as the water is deep. In the same way, he says, people rise as high as their own spirit.
teachings.link: Long, deep and high all come in this one verse. The poet treats them as one kind of measure.

teachings.teaching: The Tao Te Ching says that long and short shape each other, and high and low rest on each other.
teachings.link: A pencil is long next to an eraser and short next to a broom. You know long only because there is short.

teachings.teaching: Zhuangzi says a duck's legs are short, but stretching them would hurt the duck. A crane's legs are long, but cutting them would bring the crane sorrow.
teachings.link: Short is not worse than long. Each length fits the one who has it.

science.text: Doctors measure a baby lying down. They call this the baby's length. They measure an older child standing up, and call that the child's height. When about 1,600 small children were measured both ways, they were about 7 millimetres longer lying down. A body is soft, so the two are close but not exactly the same.

Does a thing have one true length, whoever measures it? In 1905 Albert Einstein showed that a thing moving very, very fast measures shorter to someone watching it pass. At the speeds of everyday life the change is far too small to notice.

other_view.view: They say tall and long are not just two names for one thing. Tall also tells you which way the thing points: up. And they say length was there before any words. Two sticks either match or they do not, whatever people call them. People made the words. People did not make one stick longer than the other.

practice.title: A short breath and a long breath
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Take a short breath in, and let it out. Now take a long, slow breath in, and let it out slowly. Do it once more: one short breath, one long breath. Open your eyes. Which breath was longer? You could not put the two breaths side by side. So how did you know?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Take one short breath. Then take one long, slow breath. Which was longer? How do you know?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that young children see length differently from grown-ups? This card tells the true story of three scientists and two sticks.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, grown-ups thought that comparing two sticks was something anyone could do by looking. If a child knew the word 'longer', the child saw length just as a grown-up does. In the 1940s, in Geneva in Switzerland, three scientists tested this. They were Jean Piaget, Bärbel Inhelder and Alina Szeminska. They put two sticks of the same length side by side. Each child agreed that the sticks matched. Then, while the child watched, they pushed one stick a little ahead and asked again. Many children under six or seven now said the pushed stick was longer. They looked at the end that stuck out, and not at the other end. Older children said, 'You only moved it.' The three scientists wrote about these tests in a book that came out in French in 1948 and in English in 1960. Later scientists found that the way the question is asked can change a child's answer. So they still argue about what the young children were really thinking.
how_we_found_out.who: Jean Piaget, Bärbel Inhelder and Alina Szeminska
how_we_found_out.when: The 1940s. Their book came out in French in 1948 and in English in 1960.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Anyone who knows the word 'longer' can tell which of two sticks is longer by looking. The tests showed this was wrong. Many young children judged by the end that stuck out, until they learned to look at both ends.

playtest: Walked through every flow as a family of two in a flat. The Line-Up Test needs a spoon and a pencil that differ by about a finger-width, two straws that really match, and wool that is not tugged, because wool stretches. The straw and string results are certain. The guesses are what vary. Longer Wins was played in the head with 1, 2 and 4 players: 12 strips of 12 different lengths, so no round can tie, and a tie in strips is settled by trains. The pencil hunt uses 10 things most homes have. Moong tails usually show by the third morning in warm weather, and the project says what to do if they are late. The shadow activity needs sun and is not in the core path. Step minutes add up to each part's minutes. Facts looked up on the web while writing: the 2006 ant test (10-metre walk, stilts, about 15 metres), the WHO figure of about 7 millimetres between lying length and standing height in 1,625 children, the muzham for jasmine strings, Madurai malli's protected name in 2013, the two-stick test and the 1960 English book, Fick 1851 and that the effect is still not fully explained, Thirukkural 595, Tao Te Ching 2 and Zhuangzi chapter 8. Not looked up, written from general knowledge: 1948 for the French edition of the Piaget book, the age 'under six or seven', that later studies found the wording of the question matters, that ants who walked both ways on stilts got home correctly, Einstein 1905 and fast things measuring shorter, the Hindi word lamba for both long and tall, the Birbal line story, that a tumbler's rim is about twice its height, the tailor and cricket-bat examples, the smallest-length idea in physics, the Mattuthavani flower market and the Leo Lionni book.
